overview: Assiniboine history includes family-based communities, far-reaching trade and continuing traditions of skilled making and teaching. Nakoda and Nakota are names people use for themselves; individual communities have their own histories.

periods.title: Earlier history and the limits of written records
periods.summary: Assiniboine history precedes the European written encounters discussed here. The map’s opening date does not establish a founding event or the precise location of every community.

periods.title: Trade across the northern Plains
periods.summary: European reports name Assiniboine people from the seventeenth century. Communities participated in trading routes linking the northern Plains, Hudson Bay and Missouri villages. These networks crossed many peoples’ territories.

periods.title: Fort Union trade and epidemic loss
periods.summary: Fort Union opened in 1828 with Assiniboine permission, becoming an important trading place. Smallpox brought along the Missouri devastated communities in 1837. The army dismantled the post in 1867.

periods.title: Treaties and smaller land bases
periods.summary: Colonial governments increasingly confined communities to reserves and reservations. Carry the Kettle ancestors joined Treaty 4 in 1877; Fort Belknap’s 1888 reservation followed major territorial losses. These were different local histories, not one surrender by all Assiniboine people.

periods.title: Continuing nations and shared institutions
periods.summary: Assiniboine and Gros Ventre communities maintained a shared government at Fort Belknap. Fort Peck is home to distinct Assiniboine and Sioux nations. Shared institutions did not erase those identities.

periods.title: Heritage care and teaching across generations
periods.summary: Fort Peck established its Cultural Resources Department in 1995. Its work combines museum care, archaeological protection, research and education, within the continuing life of its communities.

sections.title: Families, food and a portable home

items.text: Assiniboine bands comprised families who camped together, often linked through marriage and other kinship, according to historian David Reed Miller. Membership could change and new bands could form. A camp was also a political community.
Buffalo supported more than dinner: meat provided food, while hides supplied clothing and tipi covers. People also used many other food sources; this was not a buffalo-only menu.
The National Park Service describes cooking by placing fire-heated stones in water. Heat travelled with the stones into the vessel. In this kitchen, the hot part could arrive inside the pot.

Assiniboine traders exchanged meat and pelts with Missouri River villagers, including Mandan and Hidatsa people, for crops such as corn, beans and squash. Dinner could depend on relationships reaching well beyond one camp.

sections.title: What objects and pictures can tell us

items.text: Excavations at Fort Union recovered a bone comb, fishhook, metal bell, ornaments and gunflints. These finds reveal grooming, fishing, decoration and weapons at a nineteenth-century trading place. They do not identify the Assiniboine person, other visitor or post resident who owned each object.

George Catlin painted Assiniboin Woman and Child at Fort Union in 1832. His accompanying account described hide clothing decorated with porcupine quills and elk teeth. The painting and description preserve an outsider’s view of particular clothing, not a photograph or a complete account of the sitters’ lives. Their names are not supplied in this museum record.

Joyce Growing Thunder Fogarty’s Toy Cradleboard, dated 1989, combines beadwork, leather, cloth and painted wood. Its museum label traces the form to Kiowa and Comanche cradles, while identifying her individual style. An Assiniboine-Sioux artist can learn from neighbouring traditions and create something distinctive. This is a documented modern artwork, not an excavated ancient Assiniboine cradle.

For the Give Away Horses dress featured in a 2007 Smithsonian account, Joyce Growing Thunder Fogarty sewed blue and white beads onto elk skin. She worked for ten months, often at her kitchen table. Her daughter Juanita made accessories including a belt and sewing-tool case, while granddaughter Jessica made a beaded blanket strip. This was a family collaboration with a formidable number of tiny parts.

The dress’s horses recalled Joyce’s grandfather Ben Gray Hawk. She remembered him giving away horses to honour his grandchildren, with the person who caught a released horse keeping it. Her design turned a family memory of generosity into wearable art. The account describes this family’s experience, not a rule followed at every Assiniboine celebration.

Nakóda teachers approached Indiana University’s research institute in December 2017 about new school materials. The collaboration used elders’ recorded stories and Nakóda artists’ illustrations to create early-grade books and an app. A child could hear an elder’s voice while learning with modern technology. The project described its first materials; it did not claim the entire planned school curriculum was finished.

In a 2025 account from Aaniiih Nakoda College, student Kassi Buckles read Fifteen Animals in English and Nakoda to four- and five-year-olds, then introduced counting words. The library’s collection also included work by local writers and translators such as Assiniboine educator Minerva Allen. Story time could bring language learning, animals and numbers into the same room.

Fort Peck’s Cultural Resources Department, established in 1995, looks after a museum and a landscape containing campsites, stone-working sources, rock art and historic buildings. Heritage care includes recording and protecting places, not simply putting attractive objects behind glass. Its public mission connects that work with Dakota and Nakoda culture, history, language and life.

Carry the Kettle’s ancestors joined Treaty 4 at Fort Walsh on September 25, 1877. FHQ Developments’ community history names the chiefs and explains their wish for a reserve in their Cypress Hills homeland. This Canadian history belongs alongside the Montana stories; a present-day border should not make one part of a people’s history disappear.

ending.text: Assiniboine communities continue in the United States and Canada. Land loss and reservation policies transformed political life without ending the people. Fort Belknap, Fort Peck and Carry the Kettle have distinct histories. The map’s 1500 and 1783 endpoints are not extinction dates.
